brief.head: Thinkers set the limit
brief.text: A country can be much worse than its thinkers but never better, Ajay Shah said: they set its production possibility frontier, as Havel and Walesa did. {108-C06}

brief.text: Havel told his actors that language shapes reality. Amit Varma, quoting Jackson Katz, added that the passive voice in “violence against women” leaves out who is doing it. {108-C03}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on five unlikely leaders
lead.head: Accidents will happen
body: Amit Varma opened with a test. If his friend were handed absolute power, would he take it for the good he could do, or turn it down? Ajay Shah did not hesitate: “Get a better constitution of India. What better use of absolute power?” {108-J01}

The episode was about people who never set out to hold power. The hosts had been talking about Mark Carney, governor of the Bank of England turned prime minister of Canada, and wondered how many such accidental politicians they could name.
They chose five: Carney, the Czech playwright Václav Havel, Jawaharlal Nehru, Manmohan Singh and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
## Five accidents

Carney, Shah said, was lifted by a collapse in Trudeau’s popularity and by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Canada, which sent voters to any plausible candidate who was not a right-wing conservative. Trump was “the critical divine intervention that got Mark Carney to power”. {108-S01}
Havel, barred from university as a class enemy, became a dissident, spent years in prison and then became a president who refused to wear a tie.
Nehru, Shah argued, was carried by a chain of accidents, from two world wars to Gandhi’s choice. “It takes a Gandhi to choose a Nehru,” he said. {108-S10}
Manmohan Singh, unlike Carney, was appointed at every step: Sonia Gandhi and Narasimha Rao, Shah said, had the good sense to pick him.
Zelenskyy, a comedian who had played a president on television, became one. When Russia invaded and, it is believed, assassins came for him, he refused to flee. {108-S17}
## The case for outsiders
Varma then set out four pros and three cons. The first pro is that outsiders are generalists. A career politician in India, he said, may never have had a paying job.
The second is skin in the game of the real world. Leaders cut off from daily life, he argued, produce blunders like demonetisation.
The third is that the stakes are lower. Out of power, Varma said, Carney would go back to being a consultant. Shah widened the point: a good society is one where elections are low stakes.

The fourth is that an outsider has not spent decades in the repeated game of money and power. “To survive in politics you need money, money will demand ROI,” Varma said. “It is straight away corruption.” {108-C17}
## And the case against
Outsiders know the system less well. In 1991, Varma argued, Manmohan Singh was right as finance minister, but it took Narasimha Rao, an insider for decades, to do the politics.
Shah recalled a Labour insider in Britain whose party returned to office after a long time out: “we pressed the levers of power and nothing happened.”
Outsiders may also know less policy, and want bolder gambles than a party whose career politicians face election after election.

Will Zelenskyy win an election in peacetime? Shah reminded listeners that Churchill won the war and was booted out. Varma, who sees politics as three separate games of votes, party and governance, answered: “we simply don’t know.”
Shah tied the case for outsiders to integrity. “It is not easy to turn around after a lifetime of having forged a character to become a simple deal maker,” he said.

second.label: Havel in power
second.head: Hungry for free speech
second.deck: Told whose view he had just rejected, Václav Havel did not back down
body: Václav Havel was due to meet Lee Kuan Yew, then Singapore’s leader, later that day. At a press conference, the hosts’ friend Salil Tripathi asked him about the view that free speech matters less than feeding a hungry person. {108-S06}

Havel disagreed at once. Then, as an afterthought, he asked who held that view. “The person you’re meeting this afternoon, sir,” Tripathi replied. You could hear a pin drop. Havel said he would make sure to tell Lee that he was wrong.

Meetings between heads of state are usually choreographed, said Amit Varma, who heard the story on *The Seen and the Unseen*. Havel stayed true to himself. Varma voiced Havel’s tie refusal in Hindi, a language Havel did not know. {108-J06}

quote.text: If you do not have free speech, how will a hungry person be able to say that they are hungry?

second.caption: Havel and the hungry man’s free speech

third.head: Out of touch, out of notes
body: Amit Varma wrote a series of pieces against demonetisation. One, in the Times of India, went viral: Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal tweeted it. {108-S19}

He took apart each of Narendra Modi’s reasons. The key one, he said, was that Modi had not been a player in the real world for decades: “This man has not bought something from a paan shop in fifteen years.”

In 1978, when Indira Gandhi demonetised, a thousand-rupee note was worth twelve thousand rupees in 2016 terms, he said. The 500-rupee note scrapped in 2016 was used every day, and the cash-based informal economy was devastated.
Ajay Shah recalled George H. W. Bush, astonished on camera by a supermarket barcode scanner: “This is a guy who for twenty five years had never stepped out to buy anything for himself.” {108-S20}
third.caption: demonetisation and the paan shop

p2.title: Power by accident
p2.deck: Five leaders who never planned to rule, and the case for and against outsiders in politics

sections.label: The first accident
sections.head: Trump’s gift to Mark Carney
sections.caption: Mark Carney’s improbable rise
body: Mark Carney was a normal professional central banking type, Ajay Shah said, well respected and well trusted. In 2012, after scandals in the UK, the British appointment process chose this Canadian to run the Bank of England.

It worked, Shah argued, because inflation targeting in Canada is so much like inflation targeting in the UK, with mature statistics, good models and strong research teams. “So actually then the knowledge becomes portable,” he said. {108-C01}

Back in Canada, Carney entered party politics. Trudeau’s popularity collapsed, and Trump’s threats inflamed voters. Unlike Manmohan Singh, appointed at every step, Carney won fair and square, which gives him a different level of authority. Whether he can win again when Trump matters less is, Shah said, an open question. {108-S01}
## Parties without owners
In the West, Amit Varma said, a successful banker can imagine a career in politics; he named Mitt Romney. In India, “no respectable person is actually going to think of getting into politics.”
Shah said India had paid too little attention to the party as an institution. Parties, like firms, need rules, norms, culture and a deep pool of talent. {108-C02}

~ Varma said Nehru’s Congress had been like that. When a Ram idol was placed in the Babri Masjid, the UP chief minister Govind Ballabh Pant refused Nehru’s request to remove it. Indira Gandhi, he argued, later hollowed the party out. {108-S02}

quote.text: Donald Trump is the critical divine intervention that got Mark Carney to power.

portraits.hint: Canadian prime minister, former Bank of England governor

sections.label: The second accident
sections.head: Questions he could not answer
sections.caption: the playwright who became president
body: The communists branded Václav Havel’s well-to-do family class enemies, Amit Varma said, so Havel could not study philosophy at university. He took a job there as a lab technician instead, arriving with his pockets stuffed with Kafka, Camus, Heidegger and Nietzsche.
A friend once saw him close a notebook he had been filling furiously. Its title, as Varma remembered it: “Questions I Cannot Answer”. In it Varma saw deep curiosity and deep humility. {108-S03}
His plays, such as *The Garden Party*, mock an empty bureaucratic language that strips people of character. Havel told his actors that language shapes reality.
## Prison, then presidency

After the Prague Spring of 1968 he became an outspoken dissident, and he spent four continuous years in prison, from 1979 to 1983. {#prison} His letters to his wife were collected as *Letters to Olga*. {108-R03}

After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 he became president, but would not move into the palace or wear a tie. Asked why he was dressed like that, he said: “Because I represent the people. The people are like this.” {108-S05}
~ Instead of summits, Varma said, Havel invited Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones to perform. {108-J05}

quote.text: If I am to be punished, let it be for who I am.
quote.who: Václav Havel, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The third accident
sections.head: Crusader, not careerist
sections.caption: Nehru, the accidental prime minister
body: Jawaharlal Nehru won every election, Amit Varma said, but that is not how or why he started. The freedom generation were crusaders for principles, not career politicians. Today, he said, politics is “rival mafias fighting to get that monopoly on violence”.

Ajay Shah added a selection effect. Taking on the British Empire was so costly that only the best jumped: “when you have to jump, a very high activation energy, only the best people will jump.” {108-C07}
## A writer in jail

Nehru spent nine years in British jails, Shah said, without heating or air conditioning but with books and notebooks, and without beatings. “It was pretty,” Shah began. “Luxurious jail,” Varma finished. {108-J10}

There Nehru wrote *Glimpses of World History* as letters to his daughter, which Shah read as a child, and *The Discovery of India*, which he counts among the most important theoretical books about India. {108-R14}

Shah also credited Nehru’s era with firmly separating civilian rule from the military. Liberation movements that took up guns, he said, tend to fall into cycles of violence. “The means matter.” {108-C08}
~ Gandhi chose Nehru over Rajaji mainly because Nehru was much younger, Varma noted. “So it’s ironic that Rajaji actually outlived Nehru.” {108-J09}

quote.text: Here you have a man literally fifteen minutes before the speech, scribbling on some random piece of tissue paper, and look at the writing.

sections.label: The fourth accident
sections.head: When India was a dinky country
sections.caption: Manmohan Singh and 1991
body: Manmohan Singh began as an iconoclast, Ajay Shah said. In the 1960s Indian economists agreed that India could not export; in his PhD thesis Singh was one of the first to disagree. Exporting, he argued, is shaped by incentives: prices, customs duties, exchange rates. {108-S11}

Later, stranded in Geneva to head the South-South Commission after Ronald Reagan cut off UN funding, Singh was rescued by Percy Mistry, who lent the commission a million pounds by personal cheque. {108-S12}
## Legwork in Washington

By the late-1980s balance of payments crisis, Shah said, imports had stalled and factories were closing. “At that time India was a dinky country,” he said. “Like actually nobody gave a damn about India.” {108-S13}
Singh trekked quietly between the India ED’s office, the US Treasury and the IMF. The gains of 1991 to 1993, Shah said, launched India into a different orbit.

He compared Singh with Vajpayee: decency, coalitions, good teams. Between them came 1991 to 2011, which Shah called “the most successful period in five thousand years of Indian history”. {#fivethousand}
~ Amit Varma admired his nerve too. In UPA-1, with the Left threatening to pull support over the nuclear deal, Singh said, as Varma told it: “This is one thing I’m putting my foot down on.” {108-S15}

quote.text: Success in exporting is shaped by incentives. It’s about prices, it’s about customs duties, it’s about exchange rates.

sections.label: The fifth accident
sections.head: Putin misreads the comedian
sections.caption: Putin’s three misreadings
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s, Ajay Shah said, is the most unlikely story in the world: a successful comedian who had played a president in a television series.

Since 1991, when 94 per cent of Ukrainians voted to be their own country, Russia had kept meddling, backing a pro-Russian party, with guns too. “The game of modern hybrid warfare is to pit a country against itself,” Shah said. {108-C11}
Ukraine also lacked machinery. Poland, he said, took in twenty thousand pages of EU documents on how to be a European country. {#pages} Ukraine inherited only the arbitrary violence of the USSR.
## Three misreadings

Vladimir Putin, “deeply grounded in maleness”, underestimated three things, Shah argued. He saw Zelenskyy as just a TV comedian. He looked at Western Europe’s women defence ministers and thought, “they’re women. What will they do?” And he took America’s chaotic exit from Afghanistan as weakness. {108-S16}
Amit Varma pointed out that the withdrawal was botched under Biden. The dates, Shah replied, were chosen by Trump.

~ Varma added a credential Churchill, Nehru and Havel cannot match: “Zelenskyy played the piano with his dick.” Making a fool of yourself on stage night after night, he said, also takes courage. {108-J14}

quote.text: Putin thought this guy’s just a TV comedian. What will he do?

sections.label: Pros and cons
sections.head: Four pros, three cons
sections.caption: the pros and cons of outsiders
body: Amit Varma set out four pros and three cons. The first pro: outsiders are generalists. Someone who leaves a successful career for politics, he argued, tends to have wider interests than peers happy in their lane. {108-C13}
Politics itself, he said, is three games: winning votes, rising within party and legislature, and governing. Skill at one predicts little about the others. {108-C12}
## Who tells the leader
The second pro is skin in the game. Varma would welcome even a chaiwala, “as long as you’re an actual chaiwala selling chai at a train station.”
Ajay Shah added that knowledge reaches leaders through conversation. A Havel or a Zelenskyy arrives with friends who “are not reverential because you’ve just become a head of state.” {108-C14}

On the money that elections demand, Varma recited a limerick from his days writing them for the Times of India: “A neta who loves currency notes / told me what his line of work denotes. / It is kind of funny, we steal people’s money / and use some of it to buy their votes.” {108-J18}
~ Among the cons, outsiders know the system less well. Varma’s classic example was the 1991 partnership: “Narasimha Rao could do the politics and Manmohan could do the economics.” {108-C18}

quote.text: A politician who comes to government is not playing one game, they are playing three different games.

side.boxText: Amit Varma urged listeners to read all of Havel’s plays, available in English, and his extended essay *The Power of the Powerless*, whose latest edition carries an introduction by Timothy Snyder. His memoir *To the Castle and Back* is “also a wonderful book”. {108-R05}

contQuote.text: So a good society is one where elections are low stakes. So Kelkar always says that in a good society, politicians should go out of office, but never out of power.

p3.title: Tales of the unlikely
p3.deck: Four moments when accidental politicians showed what they were made of

stories.start: just like the Afghan regime had melted away when the Taliban came in
stories.end: And he chose to dig in and stay.
stories.caption: Zelenskyy’s choice to stay
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the night Russia came for Zelenskyy
stories.head: The comedian who would not leave
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy started out in showbiz, a very successful comedian who played a president in a television series. Then he became one. Seen as a clean figure outside the usual mess, with a campaign heavy on social media and the internet, he won 73 per cent of the vote. {#vote}
He was a little clueless, Ajay Shah said, and made many mistakes in the early days.

When Russia invaded in February 2022, Shah, like everyone else, expected his government to melt away, as Afghanistan’s had before the Taliban. An armoured thrust from Belarus was aimed at Kyiv. Shah thought Zelenskyy would run to Lviv, or lead a government in exile from Poland.
It is believed that on the first night three separate assassination teams came for his house. {#teams} He had a wife and two small children with him.
He woke up the next morning and said he was not leaving. Offered a way out, he said: “My place is here, I need ammunition, not a ride.” {108-S17}
Amit Varma tried a punchier version: “I want ammo.” Shah held firm. “The exact line is my place is here, I need ammunition, not a ride.”

~ One by one, Western countries saw that Ukraine would stand. “Would you really send a lot of military kit to somebody who is about to fold?” Shah asked. He thinks Zelenskyy made the right calls every step of the way.
stories.why: Allies commit only when a leader has the stomach for a fight. Roosevelt once sent a trusted adviser, dying of cancer, to Moscow to judge whether Stalin would stand and fight. The reply was short: yes. {108-S18}
stories.postscript: Zelenskyy rallied his people, Shah said, much as Churchill “picked up the words of the English language and hurled them into battle”. {108-J15}

stories.start: During his time as a dissident in nineteen seventy seven he comes out
stories.end: That staying silent is also taking a side.
stories.caption: the signatory who hesitated
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Charter 77 and a hesitant signatory
stories.head: The side she had already taken
body: In 1977 Václav Havel co-wrote Charter 77. He wanted a lot of people to sign it, Amit Varma said, so that it would seem the people of Czechoslovakia all believed in it.
He went to one woman, a fellow traveller. She agreed with him, she said, but signing would be dangerous, and she was not sure she should take a side.
“You have already taken a side,” Havel told her, “just not the one that you think you have.” She signed. {108-S04}

~ Varma heard in it the line attributed to Edmund Burke: evil triumphs when good men stand by and do nothing. Havel came back to the idea in 2008, campaigning for the Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo to get the Nobel Prize: the crimes of the twentieth century, he said, began when good men stayed silent. {108-C04}

quote.text: Staying silent is also taking a side.

stories.start: so he was prime minister and uh a letter appeared in the Hindustan Times
stories.end: has become too powerful and this is not a healthy state of affairs
stories.caption: the Chanakya letter
stories.head: Et tu, Jawaharlal?
body: While Jawaharlal Nehru was prime minister, Ajay Shah said, a letter in the Hindustan Times warned that he was becoming a Julius Caesar.
Power had been concentrated in him, it said. He was surrounded by sycophants and dismissed people with a wave of his hand. Readers should get together and dethrone him. It was signed Chanakya.

Some years later it turned out that the author was Nehru himself. “Can you imagine a sitting prime minister of India publishing an article saying that this Prime Minister has become too powerful and this is not a healthy state of affairs,” Shah said. {108-S08}
~ It is his favourite Nehru story. Generations from now, Shah said, people will scarcely believe that such a person walked the earth.
stories.why: A sitting leader sounding the alarm about his own power is the opposite of a politician’s instinct. Shah also admired Nehru’s ease with himself: a happy man who joked about himself and needed no strongman pose. {108-C09}

stories.start: we get to uh interregnum where Manmon Singh was not a finance minister
stories.end: And he just took the trouble of coming and participating in these things.
stories.caption: Manmohan Singh’s quiet decency
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Manmohan Singh he met
stories.head: From the back row to the front
body: Between his spells in power, Manmohan Singh was a private citizen in Delhi. Ajay Shah, then a young researcher in Bombay invited to give talks, kept seeing him slip into a back seat, listen, and say almost nothing.

In 2019 Vijay Kelkar asked Singh to release the first edition of *In Service of the Republic*, the book he wrote with Shah. Singh was unwell, and declined to be announced as chief guest in case he could not come. {108-R24}
Then, without any announcement, he came, sat in the front row, shook Shah’s hand and said: “This is a very important book, thank you for writing it.” {108-S14}
~ In those Delhi talks, Shah recalled, Singh spoke up only once, to disagree. “He never made it uncomfortable. He never threw his weight around.”
stories.why: Shah sees this quiet decency as Manmohan Singh’s method: decades spent learning how India’s institutions work, coalitions built gently and a climate of opinion slowly moved. “That’s how a paradigm shifts,” he said.
